input.raw_text: Markets here have never fallen this hard, this fast. After Sunday's surprise primary handed Alberto Fernández a fifteen-point victory over President Macri, the peso collapsed as much as thirty percent, trading past sixty to the dollar before paring losses, and sovereign bonds are down twenty cents with yields careering toward fifty percent. The Merval's plunge is among the worst single-day drops for any index in years, far uglier in dollars. Country risk has spiked above seventeen hundred basis points, pricing in a restructuring of the record IMF program Macri took and Fernández called usurious on the campaign trail. The central bank burned reserves today, auctioning dollars into a void, and still the selling came. I am watching banks and energy names — Grupo Galicia, YPF, Pampa — trade like lottery tickets, because nobody knows what policy looks like under a Fernández government. The unknown is the entire trade.
input.summary: Argentina experienced an extreme cross-market dislocation after Alberto Fernández defeated President Macri by fifteen points in the primary, with sharp peso depreciation, steep sovereign bond and equity losses, surging country risk, ineffective reserve intervention, and pronounced uncertainty about future economic policy.

interpretation.summary: The Argentine equity observations weakly support a broad bear-regime parameter state through the combination of a historic index decline and extreme sector instability. The remaining records require behaviors, measurements, horizons, models, or asset coverage that the packet does not supply.

citations.text: Regime-conditional return distribution shift in international equity returns: normal regime characterized by mean monthly return ~0.90% and volatility ~2.81%; bear regime characterized by mean monthly return ~0.13% (near zero) and volatility ~5.04% (~80% higher than normal). Observable as a bimodal or multi-modal return distribution when regimes are mixed, with the bear component dominating the left tail. Filtered regime probabilities from the Hamilton filter provide the real-time signal for which regime parameter set is active. Estimated at monthly frequency on world equity index data (MLE, Ang-Bekaert 2004 Tables 2-3). regime_conditional_mean_return; regime_conditional_return_volatility; filtered_regime_probability; bear_regime_volatility_ratio The ~80% higher bear-regime volatility (5.04% vs. 2.81%) and near-zero bear mean (0.13% vs. 0.90%) are the key quantitative observables. These parameter values provide calibration anchors for regime detection models applied to international equity markets.

A two-regime Markov-switching model identifies a normal regime (monthly mean μ=0.90%, volatility σ=2.81%) and a bear regime (monthly mean μ=0.13%, volatility σ=5.04%) in international equity returns. The bear regime exhibits approximately 80% higher volatility and near-zero mean returns compared to the normal regime. Tables 2 and 3, p.5-6. Estimated on world equity index data at monthly frequency. Normal regime corresponds to typical equity conditions; bear regime captures high-volatility drawdown periods. Transition probabilities govern regime persistence.

matched_states.state_summary: A two-state Markov-switching market condition for international equity returns characterized by empirically estimated regime-level parameters: normal regime (monthly mean μ=0.90%, volatility σ=2.81%) and bear regime (monthly mean μ=0.13%, volatility σ=5.04%). The bear regime exhibits approximately 80% higher volatility and near-zero mean returns relative to the normal regime. Transition probabilities govern regime persistence; the Hamilton filter provides real-time probability estimates of the active regime. Estimated on world equity index data at monthly frequency (Ang and Bekaert 2004, Tables 2-3).
